title: Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every subset of taps versus precomputing max reach per position and a Jump-Game-II-style greedy sweep.

sections.title: Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden

content.title: Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden

blocks.text: Problem Summary: There is a garden along the x-axis from 0 to n. There are n+1 taps, tap i (at position i) able to water the range [i - ranges[i], i + ranges[i]] if opened. Return the MINIMUM number of taps that need to be opened to water the entire garden [0, n], or -1 if it is impossible.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Each tap covers an interval; cover the whole garden with the fewest taps\"","This is exactly \"minimum number of intervals to cover a range,\" solved via a greedy jump-game-style sweep"],["Each position has a maximum reach if a tap were opened there","Track the farthest reachable point achievable from any position within the current reach"]]}

blocks.text: Each tap, if opened, covers a specific interval. The task is equivalent to selecting the minimum number of these intervals so their union covers [0, n] entirely, a classic "minimum interval cover" problem, solvable with the same greedy technique used in the Jump Game family of problems.

blocks.title: Analogy: Covering a Long Wall with the Fewest Overlapping Tarps
blocks.text: Picture a long wall needing full coverage by tarps, where each possible tarp placement covers a known range. Wanting the fewest tarps to fully cover the wall is the same challenge as this problem: convert each tap into its covering interval, then greedily pick the fewest intervals to cover everything.

blocks.caption: Each tap becomes a covering interval; the problem becomes "cover [0,n] with the fewest intervals"

blocks.text: Result: 1. Tap at position 1 covers [1-4, 1+4] = [-3,5], which alone covers the entire garden [0,5].

Before trying every subset of taps, notice that for each starting position, only the FARTHEST reach achievable by ANY tap whose interval STARTS at or before that position matters, exactly the same greedy insight used in the Jump Game II problem for finding the minimum number of jumps.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Each tap i covers [max(0, i-ranges[i]), i+ranges[i]]; precomputing, for every possible LEFT endpoint l, the maximum RIGHT endpoint achievable by any tap starting at or before l gives a "max reach from l" array.

Observation 2: This transforms the problem into a Jump-Game-like structure: from any current position, the "next reachable frontier" is the maximum of maxReach[l] for all l within the current covered range.

Observation 3: A greedy sweep, tracking the current covered boundary and the farthest next boundary achievable, incrementing a tap counter every time the sweep must extend beyond the current boundary, finds the minimum number of taps needed.

Observation 4: If at any point the sweep reaches a position beyond the farthest achievable boundary (a gap that cannot be covered), the answer is -1, since no combination of taps can bridge that gap.

This leads to precomputing the max reach achievable starting from each position, then a greedy jump-game-style sweep counting the minimum taps needed to cover [0,n], returning -1 if a gap is ever found.
Try every subset of taps (or recursively try opening each tap and checking coverage), tracking the minimum subset size whose union covers [0,n].

items: Recursively decide, for each tap, whether to open it or not.
For each complete decision, check whether the union of opened taps' intervals covers the entire [0,n] range.
Track the minimum count of opened taps among all valid (fully covering) combinations.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every subset directly finds the true minimum, guaranteed correct.
This costs exponential time (2^(n+1) subsets), utterly infeasible for n up to 10^4.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential, O(2^n times n).
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: completely infeasible at scale; recognizing this as a "minimum intervals to cover a range" problem allows a greedy O(n) solution instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why trying every subset is unnecessary: this is structurally identical to the Jump Game II "minimum jumps to reach the end" problem, just phrased with intervals instead of jump ranges.

Precomputing max reach per position: for each tap, compute its covering interval [l, r]; build an array maxReach where maxReach[l] is the LARGEST r achievable by any tap whose interval starts at l (taking the max if multiple taps share the same l).

The greedy sweep: track curEnd (the farthest position covered so far) and nextEnd (the farthest position reachable using one more tap); as the sweep index passes curEnd, increment the tap count and update curEnd to nextEnd; if the sweep index ever exceeds nextEnd, no tap combination can bridge the gap, return -1.

The core idea: precompute max reach per starting position, then the exact same greedy technique as Jump Game II finds the minimum number of taps.

Precompute maxReach[l] for every possible left endpoint l. Sweep positions 0 to n, tracking curEnd and nextEnd; increment the tap count whenever the sweep passes curEnd, updating curEnd to nextEnd. Return -1 if the sweep ever exceeds nextEnd.
maxReach[0] = 5 (from tap 1). Sweep: at i=0, curEnd=0, so open a tap (taps=1), curEnd becomes nextEnd=5; since 5>=n=5, done. Total taps = 1.

blocks.caption: Precompute max reach per position, then a greedy jump-game-style sweep counts the minimum taps

blocks.text: Precomputing the max reach achievable from every starting position condenses all taps' coverage information into a single array, exactly mirroring the Jump Game II setup. The greedy sweep correctly counts the minimum number of taps: it only "spends" a new tap when forced to (the current position exceeds everything covered so far), and always extends coverage as far as possible with each tap used, which is provably optimal for interval-covering problems of this form. A gap that cannot be bridged (current position exceeds the farthest reachable frontier) correctly signals impossibility.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the maxReach array.

blocks.text: Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden is a strong example of recognizing that a seemingly novel problem is structurally identical to the well-known Jump Game II, once each tap is reframed as a covering interval.

items: Forgetting to clamp the left endpoint of a tap's interval at 0 (i - ranges[i] can be negative).
Not handling the -1 impossible case, incorrectly assuming the garden can always be fully watered.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "cover a range with the fewest intervals from a given set", think: precompute max reach per position, then the same greedy sweep as Jump Game II.

items: How would you also report WHICH taps to open, not just the minimum count?
How would this change if taps had an associated cost, requiring a weighted minimum instead?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Trying every subset of taps costs exponential time; the precompute-and-greedy-sweep approach costs O(n) time and O(n) space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: precompute max reach per position, then a Jump-Game-II-style greedy sweep for minimum interval coverage.
Core Idea: convert each tap to its covering interval; track curEnd and nextEnd, incrementing a tap counter whenever the sweep passes curEnd.
Time: exponential for trying every subset, O(n) for the optimized greedy sweep.
Space: O(n) for the recursion versus the maxReach array.
Most Important Observation: this problem is structurally identical to Jump Game II, once taps are reframed as covering intervals.
Interview Difficulty: a clever reduction problem rewarding recognition of the underlying Jump Game structure.
One line memory trick: precompute max reach per position; greedily extend coverage, counting taps used.
